strengths: Novel metric-based prompting strategy that replaces explicit degradation labels with automatically computed spatial-spectral metrics, addressing a practical limitation of prior prompt-based methods
Rigorous and transparent metric selection pipeline starting from 25 candidates and filtering based on interpretability, coverage, and discriminability with Random Forest validation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 datasets (3 natural, 5 remote sensing) with both unified training and zero-shot generalization protocols, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong baselines
Strong zero-shot generalization results, particularly 2.10 dB improvement on unseen Poisson denoising, suggesting metrics effectively capture underlying degradation patterns
Well-designed ablation studies (Tables 4-6) validating component contributions, including DP effectiveness (+4.20 dB), SSAM benefit (+1.41 dB), and routing strategy comparison
Efficient implementation with comparable parameters and competitive inference time compared to other unified restoration methods, with minimal overhead from DP computation
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, particularly Figure 2 demonstrating metric discriminability and Figure 3 illustrating the architecture
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: SSAM (Eq. 6) is a straightforward weighted combination of spatial/spectral features (standard practice), and DAMoE follows conventional top-k routing without innovation; main novelty confined to prompting strategy

Insufficient validation of core assumption: the paper assumes metrics directly inform restoration strategies but never explicitly models or validates the connection between metric values and optimal expert/SSAM selection

Questionable generalization claims: metrics selected from only 1,000 HSIs with 5 predefined degradation types; zero-shot evaluation on only 2 unseen degradations on single dataset (CAVE); no analysis of failure modes or metric robustness to errors

Domain-specific metric design reduces applicability: the 6 metrics are engineered specifically for HSI degradations, with unclear generalization to natural images or other imaging modalities; approach may not extend beyond the 5 training degradation types

Incomplete experimental analysis: multi-task training shows marginal/inconsistent improvements (Table 10); zero-shot evaluation limited to small CAVE dataset; sensitivity analysis on metric normalization and computation errors absent; comparison with MP-HSIR [45] needs clarification on prompt differences

Missing technical justification: metric normalization strategy unspecified; routing function design not ablated; why 6 metrics specifically not justified; no analysis of handling spatially-varying degradations or metric computation robustness
Misleading efficiency claims: inference time (133.18 ms) is 4.6× slower than InstructIR baseline (28.84 ms); efficiency advantage mainly over other MoE methods; DP computation cost not discussed

Limited zero-shot evaluation scope: only 2 unseen degradations on single dataset weakens 'exceptional generalization' claims; no evaluation on larger remote sensing datasets or natural images; no analysis of degradation types where metrics fail

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 datasets with 5+ restoration tasks, including zero-shot generalization tests demonstrating practical applicability
Well-motivated problem addressing a real limitation of existing methods: the difficulty of obtaining explicit degradation priors in real-world scenarios
Systematic and transparent metric selection pipeline clearly documented with justification based on interpretability, coverage, and discriminability
Strong quantitative results with SOTA performance across multiple tasks (Table 2) and meaningful improvements in zero-shot generalization (2.10 dB for Poisson denoising)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-7) effectively demonstrating the contribution of each component and detailed analysis of routing strategies
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 2) showing metric-based degradation type separation and distribution analysis
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core components are not novel—metrics are standard image processing operations, spatial-spectral feature extraction uses standard transformers+1D convolutions, and MoE routing for image restoration is established (MoCE-IR, CVPR2025). The main contribution is combining these in a straightforward manner

Misleading framing of metrics as 'prompts': Degradation metrics are computed from input images, making them input-dependent features rather than external guidance/prompts. This differs fundamentally from textual prompts or degradation labels, yet the distinction is not clearly articulated

Weak justification for metric-based routing superiority: Figure 2(b) shows moderate classification accuracy (confusion matrix has non-negligible off-diagonal entries). No empirical comparison demonstrating that continuous metric values fundamentally outperform continuous degradation-type parameterization

SSAM lacks substantive analysis: The module simply learns two scalar weights λ_s and λ_c to interpolate between spatial and spectral features. No visualization or interpretation of learned weights across degradation types, and marginal gains (1.41 dB, Table 4) raise questions about necessity

Modest zero-shot improvements: Motion deblurring gains only 0.52 dB over PromptIR (31.05 vs 30.53). While Poisson denoising shows 2.10 dB improvement, these gains are not sufficient to conclusively validate metric-based prompting superiority

Missing computational cost breakdown: Table 7 reports total FLOPs but omits the computational cost specifically attributable to metric extraction and projection, limiting practical deployment insights

Evaluation protocol concerns: Remote sensing data uses 80/20 split from single images, potentially confounding spatial correlation effects with degradation handling capability. The protocol doesn't reflect true generalization

Insufficient theoretical grounding: The paper assumes (but doesn't formally justify) that images with similar metric values require similar restoration strategies. Why should metric similarity correlate with restoration strategy similarity?

Multi-task learning instabilities unexplained: Table 10 shows degradation in Gaussian denoising under multi-task learning (41.47→41.06 dB) compared to single-task. Paper provides no analysis of task conflicts or when multi-task collaboration helps vs. hurts

Limited exploration of alternatives: The paper doesn't investigate whether simpler alternatives (e.g., end-to-end learned degradation classifiers, or fixed spatial-spectral weights) would achieve comparable performance, limiting impact claims

strengths: Novel metric-based degradation prompting that eliminates explicit degradation labels—a practical advance over prior work requiring task-specific instructions or degradation type labels

Well-motivated and validated metric selection pipeline: principled reduction from 25→16→12→6 metrics with clear interpretability criteria and Random Forest validation showing near-perfect separation of degradation types
Strong experimental results: SOTA performance across 5 known degradation tasks with exceptional zero-shot generalization (e.g., +2.10dB on unseen Poisson denoising vs. previous best)
Comprehensive evaluation across 8 datasets (3 natural + 5 remote sensing HSI) with unified training protocol and dual evaluation strategies (unified training and zero-shot)
Thorough ablation studies validating each component (DP: +4.20dB, SSAM: +1.41dB) and demonstrating plug-and-play transferability to other architectures (+1.00-1.99dB improvements)
Thoughtful domain-specific design: spatial-spectral metrics and SSAM architecture appropriately tailored to HSI's unique characteristics versus general image restoration
Practical value: addresses real-world HSI restoration where degradation types and parameters are typically unknown, improving applicability over label-dependent methods
Competitive computational efficiency: second-lowest FLOPs and inference time among unified methods while significantly outperforming the most efficient baseline (InstructIR)
weaknesses: Incomplete architectural specifications: projection function f_proj (Eq. 3) lacks formal definition; metric-to-embedding transformation procedure stated but not detailed, limiting reproducibility despite promised code release

Metric validation scope limited to ARAD natural images; generalization to remote sensing HSIs with different sensors and spectral ranges not explicitly validated despite claiming domain-agnostic approach

Domain separation strategy: training separate models for natural vs. remote sensing HSIs reduces generalization claims; no cross-domain transfer experiments (natural→remote sensing or vice versa) provided

Limited zero-shot generalization scope: only 2 unseen degradation types (motion deblurring, Poisson denoising) tested on single dataset (CAVE); comprehensive evaluation across diverse degradations and multiple datasets needed to support robustness claims
Missing critical baseline: no comparison with learned degradation estimation methods (e.g., auxiliary prediction network); unclear whether fixed metrics outperform learned representations

Insufficient justification for key design choices: (1) load balancing noise ε in Eq. 3 not ablated, (2) metric redundancy threshold ρ=0.8 not justified, (3) finding that k=1 experts outperforms k≥2 explained speculatively without deeper analysis
Metric sensitivity not explored: robustness to metric computation parameters (FFT window, patch sizes, local vs. global computation) not investigated

Modest improvements on some benchmarks relative to recent baselines: Gaussian denoising shows marginal gains; improvements sometimes attributable to multi-task training rather than metric-based routing specifically

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across 8 datasets, 5 unified + 2 zero-shot tasks with extensive ablations
Well-motivated problem with systematic metric selection pipeline (3-stage filtering on 1,000 HSI samples)
Strong empirical results: SOTA on unified tasks, impressive zero-shot generalization (31.05dB motion blur vs 30.53dB PromptIR), handles heterogeneous degradations
Thorough analysis of expert specialization and activation patterns (Fig. 12), computational efficiency analysis (Table 6), and realistic scenario evaluation (E.10)
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging domain-gap issues and restricted generalization scope
weaknesses: Weak metric-degradation correlations undermine core claims: only 7/9 pairs exceed r>0.4, band missing shows r≈0.0 with HFER, contradicting 'reliable characterization' argument
Domain-gap requiring separate natural/remote-sensing models directly contradicts 'universal representation' claims and significantly limits practical impact
Limited novelty: primarily combines existing MoE + attention architectures; main contribution (metrics-as-prompts) is incremental
Questionable zero-shot scope: only 2 unseen degradations (motion blur, Poisson noise) that are variations of seen types, not fundamentally novel physics
Missing critical details: code URL blank in abstract, metric extraction computational cost not itemized in Table 6, Random Forest selection unjustified, statistical significance testing absent
Modest performance improvements: many gains 0.2-0.5dB within measurement noise; Table 9 shows weak multi-task collaboration benefits; Table 18 shows 12-metric baseline matches 6-metric performance
Weak expert specialization: Fig. 12 shows soft mixing (Expert 1: λ_s=0.63, λ_c=0.37) contradicting 'clear polarization' claims; top-k=1 (Table 11) conflicts with MoE design philosophy
Metric space insufficiency not addressed: no formal analysis of coverage, worst-case failures, or robustness to out-of-distribution degradations

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 HSI datasets and 7 degradation types with extensive ablation studies in supplementary material
Interpretability-focused approach using explicit spatial-spectral metrics instead of black-box embeddings, with clear physical interpretations provided
Consistent empirical improvements over recent baselines (PromptIR, InstructIR, MP-HSIR) across multiple restoration tasks
Promising zero-shot generalization to unseen degradation types with 0.52-2.10 dB improvements (Table 3)
Thorough supplementary material with expert specialization visualizations, routing ablations, and multi-expert analysis
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines existing techniques (metrics conditioning, MoE, attention) in straightforward manner without significant innovation
Core metric-generalization claim is unproven: Figure 2 validates only 3 of 6 metrics; Figure 7 shows moderate (0.3-0.5) Pearson correlations, not strong relationships
Interpretability claims are contradicted by design: routing function (Eq. 3) processes metrics through learned MLPs/softmax, negating interpretability advantage and approximating implicit methods

Zero-shot generalization is limited: motion blur and Poisson noise are mathematically similar to training degradations (Gaussian blur/noise); no evaluation on fundamentally different degradation families
Requires separate models for natural vs. remote sensing data, contradicting unified framework claim and undermining generalization arguments
Metric selection pipeline may overfit to training degradations: 25→16→12→6 metrics filtering on 1,000 images with 5 degradation types; no cross-validation on independent dataset

Experimental concerns: small training sets (900 images for ARAD), no statistical significance testing or error bars, no justification for top-k=1 expert routing reducing MoE to single expert selection
Limited analysis of failure modes: acknowledges need for additional metrics on novel degradations (Limitations) but provides no empirical demonstration beyond one extreme combined scenario

Router adaptivity limited: global metric computation via GAP and lack of spatial information; while E.3 claims to handle heterogeneous degradations, this demonstrates limitations rather than validation
Performance improvements often modest (1-2 dB PSNR in many cases) despite architectural complexity; code not reproducible (missing GitHub URL); degradation formulas referenced but not provided

strengths: Well-motivated approach using interpretable spatial-spectral metrics as degradation prompts, clearly positioned between inflexible explicit priors and opaque black-box methods
Rigorous and systematic metric selection pipeline (three-stage filtering from 25 to 6 candidates) with solid empirical validation using Random Forest classification
Comprehensive experimental validation across 8 datasets, 7 degradation types, with extensive ablation studies demonstrating component effectiveness
Strong and consistent SOTA results with significant zero-shot generalization improvements (+0.52dB motion blur, +2.10dB Poisson noise vs. PromptIR)
Excellent interpretability compared to black-box methods, with clear visualizations of expert specialization (Figure 12) and metric-severity correlations (Figure 7)
Technically sound design with principled degradation-aware routing (Eq. 3) and well-motivated SSAM architecture with learnable spatial-spectral fusion coefficients
Exceptional supplementary material including real-world evaluation, spatially heterogeneous degradations, extreme combined degradations, and computational scalability analysis
weaknesses: Metric generalization validation limited to 500 patches with 5 degradation types; validation on all 7 test types is incomplete. Pearson correlations show several metric pairs <0.4, suggesting metrics may not universally capture degradation aspects

Fundamental contradiction: requires separate training for natural vs. remote sensing domains due to domain gaps, undermining claimed 'unified' framework. No solution or domain-adaptation exploration provided
Modest performance improvements over strong baselines (typically 1-2 dB PSNR). Zero-shot motion blur shows only +0.52dB over PromptIR, raising questions about practical significance

Expert specialization not fully convincing: single-expert routing (Table 11, 51.43 dB) outperforms multi-expert activation (50.84 dB), contradicting MoE motivation. Figure 12 shows moderate polarization, potentially an artifact

Zero-shot generalization limited to motion blur and Poisson noise—both variants of trained blur/noise types. Generalization to truly novel degradations (rain streaks, haze, compression artifacts) not demonstrated
Real-world evaluation (Table 20) shows modest improvements (20.33 vs 18.45 dB for PromptIR), suggesting challenges in practical deployment
Limited metric analysis: no justification for selecting 6 over 8-10 metrics; metrics are standard image quality measures without HSI-specific innovation
Missing failure case analysis and discussion of image properties that challenge the method
Dense presentation relying heavily on supplementary material (5 main + 20 appendix pages); distinction between DP and black-box embeddings could be clearer
